description: We are SEEDRA, a team of young innovators passionate about technology and sustainable agriculture. Our mission is to empower Peruvian farmers through NASA satellite data, creating intelligent solutions with global impact.
summary:
SEEDRA is an agroclimatic intelligence platform that integrates data from NASA POWER, FAO hydrological models, and ancestral Andean agricultural knowledge to assess climate risks and optimize crop rotation strategies.

The system processes variables such as precipitation, temperature, solar radiation, humidity, and wind to develop agroclimatic analysis at the plot level. It implements the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method to estimate reference evapotranspiration, FAO-33 to simulate yield response to water stress, and the SPI index, adjusted through the Gamma distribution, to identify drought conditions.

Its four-season planner incorporates the ancestral Aynoca system, using agronomic compatibility rules between crops to compare rotation sequences, considering diversification, biological nitrogen fixation, and fallow periods.

Initially applied to the Puno Altiplano, SEEDRA transforms satellite information and scientific models into indicators, simulations, and agricultural decision-making alternatives.
details:
1. What exactly does it do?

SEEDRA is a data-driven agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers make more informed crop selection and rotation decisions under changing climatic conditions.

By integrating NASA POWER agroclimatic datasets, water-balance models, historical climate analysis, and principles inspired by the ancestral Andean agricultural system known as Aynoca, SEEDRA transforms complex environmental information into practical indicators and agricultural planning alternatives.

Specifically, the platform:

Retrieves and processes historical daily agroclimatic data from NASA POWER for user-selected agricultural locations.

Analyzes precipitation, temperature, solar radiation, wind speed, relative humidity, and surface and root-zone soil moisture indicators.

Estimates crop water requirements and simulates potential crop yield responses to water stress.

Evaluates historical drought conditions, precipitation patterns, and frost occurrence.

Compares five crops: potatoes, quinoa, fava beans, barley, and oats.

Generates four-season crop rotation sequences using agronomic compatibility rules inspired by the ancestral Aynoca system.

Presents results through interactive maps, historical charts, agroclimatic indicators, and comparative tables.

2. How does it work?

SEEDRA follows a six-stage workflow that transforms historical environmental information into agricultural decision-support tools.

2.1. Geospatial Plot Selection

Users select an agricultural location through an interactive map developed with Folium. The project initially focuses on the Puno Altiplano in Peru, allowing users to explore different districts or select custom geographic coordinates.

2.2. NASA POWER Data Acquisition and Processing

The platform connects to the NASA POWER API to retrieve historical daily datasets, including precipitation, maximum and minimum temperatures, solar radiation, wind speed, relative humidity, and surface and root-zone soil moisture indicators.

These datasets are processed and organized into time series that provide the foundation for hydrometeorological analysis and agricultural simulations.

2.3. Scientific Agroclimatic Modeling

SEEDRA integrates three main scientific methodologies:

FAO-56 Penman-Monteith: Estimates reference evapotranspiration (ET₀) using meteorological variables and elevation. The implementation also includes Hargreaves-Samani as an alternative when sufficient information is unavailable for the primary method.

FAO-33 – Yield Response to Water: Implements a simplified root-zone water balance to estimate actual evapotranspiration (ETa), crop water requirements (ETc), and potential yield response to water stress, using crop coefficients (Kc) and yield response factors (Ky).

Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI): Applies Gamma probability distribution fitting to historical seasonal precipitation to characterize drought and wet conditions relative to historical precipitation patterns.

2.4. Historical Agricultural Season Simulation

Using historical climate records, SEEDRA reconstructs agricultural seasons to evaluate the simulated performance of five crops under different climatic conditions.

The system calculates:

Median simulated relative yield (P50).

Lower simulated relative yield scenario (P20).

Historical simulated frequency of potential yield losses due to water stress.

Seasonal precipitation and crop water demand.

Number of days with minimum temperatures at or below 0°C.

Historical trends in simulated crop yields, precipitation, and rainfall onset.

These indicators allow users to compare the simulated water-related vulnerability of different crops across historical growing seasons.

2.5. Aynoca Crop Rotation Planner

SEEDRA incorporates a four-season crop rotation planner inspired by Aynoca, an ancestral Andean agricultural system characterized by organized crop rotation and periods of land rest.

The system uses an agronomic compatibility matrix to evaluate sequences involving potatoes, quinoa, fava beans, barley, and oats.

Its predefined rules consider:

Diversification of botanical families.

Biological nitrogen fixation potential associated with legumes.

Disruption of pest and disease cycles.

Potential use of residual soil fertility.

Crop alternation and fallow periods as agronomic principles.

The planner generates crop rotation alternatives using predefined compatibility scores and historical simulation results. These alternatives are preliminary and require local agronomic validation.

2.6. Interactive Visualization and Decision Support

SEEDRA presents its results through an interactive web platform featuring:

  • Interactive maps for selecting agricultural locations.
  • Comparative tables of crops and simulated scenarios.
  • Historical climate trend charts.
  • Drought, precipitation, and soil moisture indicators.
  • Visual representations of simulated relative yields and water-related risks.
  • A simplified Farmer Mode that uses color-coded risk categories and understandable crop recommendations.

The interface also provides language options in Spanish, English, and Aymara, aiming to make agroclimatic information more accessible.

3. What benefits does it offer?

Environmental Benefits

SEEDRA supports agroclimatic risk analysis by identifying historical water-stress conditions, evaluating drought patterns, and comparing crop rotation alternatives. Its approach aims to support better-informed water management and encourage agricultural diversification.

Social Benefits

The platform makes scientific and climate information easier to interpret through interactive maps, charts, and visual indicators. Its simplified Farmer Mode allows users with limited technical knowledge to explore planting alternatives and better understand the risks identified by the system.

Economic Benefits

SEEDRA compares historical scenarios of simulated relative crop yields and potential loss frequencies, providing information that may support better-informed agricultural decisions. Future applications could help reduce farmers' economic exposure to unfavorable climatic conditions, although these benefits have not yet been validated.

Cultural and Scientific Benefits

The project integrates established agroclimatic models with principles inspired by the ancestral Aynoca agricultural system. This approach demonstrates how traditional agricultural knowledge and modern Earth observation technologies can complement each other without replacing farmers' practical experience.

4. What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, our goal is to demonstrate SEEDRA as a functional agroclimatic decision-support prototype in the Puno Altiplano. We aim to verify NASA POWER data acquisition, agroclimatic indicator processing, historical agricultural season simulations, and the generation of crop rotation alternatives.

We also seek to identify the limitations of our current models and establish a methodological foundation for future calibration and validation using local agricultural data.

In the long term, we aim to incorporate field observations related to soil properties, actual crop yields, agricultural calendars, and water availability to improve the reliability of our simulations and evaluate the practical usefulness of SEEDRA's recommendations.

Our goal is to progressively adapt SEEDRA to other agricultural regions of Peru and develop a tool that connects satellite information, scientific models, and local agricultural knowledge to strengthen resilience to climate variability.

5. What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Programming Language

  • Python: Development of the computational logic, data processing algorithms, and scientific models.

Application Development

  • Streamlit: Development of the interactive web platform and its navigation components.

Data Processing and Scientific Computing

  • Pandas: Organization and analysis of agroclimatic time series.
  • NumPy: Numerical computations and mathematical operations.
  • SciPy: Statistical analysis, probability distribution fitting, and trend analysis.

NASA Data Acquisition

  • NASA POWER API: Retrieval of historical agroclimatic information.
  • Requests: API communication and data retrieval.

Interactive Mapping

  • Folium: Geospatial mapping and location selection.
  • Streamlit-Folium: Integration of interactive maps into the web application.

Data Visualization

  • Altair: Development of statistical charts, crop comparisons, and historical trend visualizations.

Scientific Methodologies

  • FAO-56 Penman-Monteith: Estimation of reference evapotranspiration.
  • FAO-33: Estimation of crop yield response to water stress.
  • Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and Gamma Distribution: Statistical characterization of precipitation conditions.
  • Linear Regression: Exploratory analysis of historical trends.
  • Agronomic Compatibility Matrix: Evaluation of crop rotation alternatives inspired by Aynoca.

Scientific Data Sources and References

  • NASA POWER.
  • Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).
  • World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
  • SENAMHI Peru, as an agroclimatic scientific reference.

Interface and Accessibility

  • Language options in Spanish, English, and Aymara.
  • Simplified Farmer Mode with visual risk indicators.

Core Innovation

SEEDRA integrates historical NASA POWER agroclimatic data, crop water-stress modeling, and ancestral crop rotation principles into a single interactive platform.

Its innovation lies in transforming complex environmental information into understandable indicators and agricultural planning alternatives, connecting space science with traditional Andean agricultural knowledge.

SEEDRA: From space to soil, from data to decisions.
